title: The Base Rate, and Why a Good Test Can Be Wrong
quickIdea: When the cause is rare, most positive results come from the large healthy group: a test with 98% sensitivity and 99% specificity applied at 1% prevalence gives a posterior near 0.50, and at 0.1% prevalence about 0.09.
remember: The arithmetic: numerator = prevalence x sensitivity; denominator = that plus (1 - prevalence) x false-positive rate.
At 1% prevalence, 98% sensitivity and 1% false positives: 0.0098/(0.0098 + 0.0099) = 98/197, about 0.4975.
At 0.1% prevalence the same test gives 98/1097, about 0.089 - under 10 per cent, which is StatLect's robot example.
At 10% prevalence the same test gives 98/107, about 0.916. The test did not change; the population did.
The false positives scale with the size of the healthy group, so a rare disease generates more false positives than true ones however accurate the test is.
This is the base-rate fallacy: quoting the sensitivity as the posterior, which is the same error as confusing P(positive | disease) with P(disease | positive).

example.prompt: A factory robot flags a defective item with probability 0.98 when the item really is defective, and stays silent with probability 0.99 when it is not. One item in a thousand is defective. The robot flags an item - what is the probability that it is right?
example.work: Prior 0.001, likelihood 0.98, so the defective-and-flagged branch is 0.00098. The not-defective branch is 0.999 x 0.01 = 0.00999. Evidence = 0.01097. Posterior = 0.00098/0.01097 = 98/1097, about 0.0893.
example.answer: About 0.089 - under 10 per cent, for a robot that is 98% sensitive and 99% specific.

gateAngle: No CSE previous-year question in this topic is a base-rate question, so the card is P2; its structure is GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q.22 with a much smaller prior, and that question's answer 0.50 is the same arithmetic at a prior of 1/5.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A disease has prevalence 1%. A test has sensitivity 98% and specificity 99%. A random person tests positive. What is the probability that the person has the disease?
variations.why: 0.0098/(0.0098 + 0.0099). About half the positives are false, because the 99% of the population without the disease is a hundred times larger than the 1% with it.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is 0.98 the wrong answer to the question above?
variations.answer: 0.98 is P(positive | disease), a property of the test. The question asks for P(disease | positive), which also depends on how common the disease is.
variations.why: A conditional probability is a share of its denominator. Changing which group you divide by changes the answer, and the prevalence is what makes the two groups different sizes.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: With the same test, what is the posterior probability at 10% prevalence?
variations.why: 0.098/(0.098 + 0.009). A tenfold rise in prevalence turns a coin flip into a strong conclusion.

trap.what: Treating the accuracy of a test as the probability that its verdict is right.
trap.why: Accuracy is conditional on the true state; the question is conditional on the observed verdict. Bayes' theorem is what converts one into the other, and the base rate is the conversion factor.
trap.counterexample: The 1% prevalence test: 98% sensitive, 99% specific, and only 98/197 of its positives are true positives.

check.question: At 1% prevalence with 98% sensitivity and 1% false positives, what is P(disease | positive)?
